correctness.rationale: Exact atomic-diagram recursion characterizes full first-order quantifier rank three, not an approximation. For all paths of size at least seven, the four possible rooted rank-two types are proved by pair-neighborhood extension conditions; coordinatewise Ehrenfeucht games preserve strong-product adjacency, reducing all positive sizes to twenty-eight canonical pairs. Complete explicit finite enumeration of these pairs yields twenty-two distinct exact types by two independent algorithms. The largest least-order class representative has 30 vertices and a corresponding pair is shown not equivalent to any smaller king graph.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Potential broad coverage would be a general rank-three product theorem explicitly classifying strong products, or a classification of all bounded-degree finite graphs that specializes to these board types. A Cartesian product is not the same relational structure, and its result cannot be substituted without new extension calculations.

The exact table and cross-shape collapses are not entailed by the related Cartesian-grid classification because diagonal adjacency changes atomic triple extensions. Searches for exact/alias/stronger coverage found no decisive prior implication, with risks explicitly stated.
residual_risks: A specialist older source or unpublished table could contain equivalent exact classes but be unindexed or inaccessible.
The material review of the general survey was not a full-paper comprehensive negative comparison.
A similarly structured Cartesian-grid classification exists; the current result requires a separate nontrivial strong-product computation and its substantive novelty should be evaluated accordingly.
The crossing-number article was available at abstract level only; while its announced invariant is different, whole-document absence of logical results was not established.

value.rationale: Gives the complete natural FO rank-three equivalence relation for king-move rectangular boards, with fifteen genuinely two-dimensional classes, exact cross-shape identifications (3×7 with 4×6 and 5×6 with arbitrarily large boards), and the sharp finite testing ceiling 30. These are properties of a classical strong-product graph family, not arbitrary parameter slices or mere reproduction of a known invariant. Complete classification and optimal representative bound are independently useful without a further downstream theorem.
